articles.title: Pharmacological treatments for painful neuroma: current standards and future perspectives.
articles.abstract: Chronic pain remains a major medical concern around the world. In particular, there are few treatments that are effective in providing relief from pain derived from injuries of the peripheral nervous system. An under-investigated component of peripheral nerve injury is the formation of a painful neuroma, a sensitive bulb of nerves growing from the severed nerve. Although these symptomatic neuromas can be treated surgically, pain deriving from them does not respond to most pharmacological treatments and contributes to the complexity of treating traumatic injuries like amputation. Here, we discuss the state of therapeutic care for neuroma and potential new pharmacological strategies to treat this pain. Particularly, we highlight the limitations in targeting the painful neuroma, challenges in appropriately modelling this disease state in animals and novel targets for effective analgesics.

articles.title: Targeting estrogen receptor signalling for the management of insulin resistance: From hormones to herbal modulators.
articles.abstract: Estrogen exerts a critical influence on metabolic health by modulating insulin signalling pathways via its receptors (ERα, ERβ and the G protein-coupled oestrogen receptor [GPER]). Estrogen decline, as seen postmenopausally or in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), is strongly associated with insulin resistance and the pathogenesis of Type 2 diabetes. The beneficial metabolic actions of estrogen, including enhanced insulin sensitivity, are mediated through mechanisms such as AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) activation, promotion of GLUT4 translocation, and suppression of inflammatory pathways. Conversely, decreased estrogen levels contribute to adipose tissue accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction and exacerbated insulin resistance. Current pharmacological interventions, including hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), can ameliorate insulin resistance but are accompanied by ongoing debate concerning their cardiovascular safety and oncological risk. These risks highlights the need for more targeted therapeutic strategies. Emerging agents, such as ERβ-selective agonists and GPER activators, alongside the refined application of herbal phytoestrogens, offer promising avenues to develop tissue- and receptor-specific modulators. Consequently, future pharmacological development needs to focus on harnessing these selective estrogenic pathways to achieve optimal metabolic benefits, whilst minimising off-target effects, so paving the way for precision medicine in the management of metabolic disease.

articles.title: PECAM-1 as an endothelial gateway for vascular-targeted drug delivery: structural basis, mechanotransduction, and translational opportunities.
articles.abstract: Platelet endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1/CD31) is a junctional adhesion and signaling receptor that is abundant on vascular endothelium and is also expressed on platelets and several leukocyte populations. It regulates leukocyte transendothelial migration, endothelial barrier function, mechanotransduction, platelet inhibitory signaling, and angiogenesis. Its abundant luminal expression and accessibility from the bloodstream have also made PECAM-1 an attractive target for vascular drug delivery and biomaterial engineering. This Review examines the structural features, extracellular interactions, and intracellular signaling mechanisms that determine PECAM-1 targetability. We further discuss its roles in vascular inflammation, atherosclerosis, ischemic injury, thrombosis, hematologic disorders, and cancer, distinguishing receptor blockade or activation from PECAM-1 targeted cargo delivery. Particular attention is given to delivery design, including epitope selection, ligand format, multivalency, carrier properties, intracellular trafficking, luminal anchoring, and cargo-specific requirements. We also evaluate translational factors that may determine targeting performance, including administration route, pharmacokinetics, species differences, disease-associated changes in the vascular microenvironment, manufacturing reproducibility, and patient variability. Together, current evidence supports PECAM-1 as a functional vascular receptor, an endothelial delivery address, and a bioactive interface for vascular devices, while emphasizing that successful translation requires careful matching of target biology, delivery design, therapeutic cargo, and disease context.

articles.title: Rewiring resistance in solid tumors: CAR-NK strategies for immune evasion and tumor microenvironmental barriers.
articles.abstract: Clinical translation of adoptive cellular immunotherapy in solid tumors remains constrained by a hierarchical resistance architecture comprising antigen heterogeneity, extracellular matrix (ECM) mediated transport barriers, immune suppression, and spatial exclusion. Although chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have demonstrated durable clinical responses in hematological malignancies, their efficacy in solid tumors remains limited by impaired cellular trafficking, restricted tissue penetration, heterogeneous intratumoral distribution, and profound microenvironmental suppression. Natural killer (NK) cells complement CAR-T therapy through major histocompatibility complex (MHC) independent tumor recognition, improved targeting of antigen-low tumor cells, and dynamic interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Building on these complementary properties, we introduce a Resistance-Solution Mapping Framework (RSMF) that systematically links major resistance barriers with engineering strategies designed to overcome them, while reframing engineered CAR-NK cells as programmable, living drug delivery systems. Unlike conventional reviews that catalogue engineering technologies, this framework evaluates how multi-antigen targeting, cytokine armoring, chemokine receptor engineering, and related approaches can modulate cellular pharmacokinetics, including tumor-directed trafficking, target-site accumulation and functional persistence within complex solid tumor ecosystems. We further critically assess the predictive value and translational limitations of advanced preclinical platforms, including patient-derived organoids and xenograft models, for evaluating immune-cell trafficking, matrix penetration, metabolic fitness, and therapeutic durability. Collectively, this review provides a systems-level roadmap integrating cellular engineering, tumor transport biology, and drug delivery principles to guide the rational development of next-generation CAR-NK therapies for overcoming multifactorial resistance in solid tumors.

articles.title: Therapeutic resistance in brain malignancies: mechanisms limiting drug efficacy and emerging pharmacological strategies.
articles.abstract: Therapeutic resistance in malignant brain tumors does not arise from a single molecular abnormality, but rather from the interplay among insufficient drug exposure, intrinsic and adaptive tumor-cell dependencies, cell-state plasticity, and the intracranial microenvironment. Although central nervous system (CNS)-active tyrosine kinase inhibitors, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted antibody-drug conjugates, and immune checkpoint inhibitors have improved intracranial outcomes in selected patients with brain metastases harboring actionable molecular alterations or immunologically responsive features, many mechanistically compelling strategies for glioblastoma (GBM) have yet to translate consistently into survival benefits in randomized clinical trials beyond the current standard of care. Rather than equating an association with resistance with therapeutic actionability, this Review evaluates resistance mechanisms and their potential for intervention through five linked steps: whether a drug can achieve sufficient exposure within intracranial lesions and critical resistance niches; whether the intervention produces sustained target modulation or the intended pharmacodynamic effect; whether the implicated mechanism represents a causal driver of resistance or an actionable dependency rather than merely a descriptive correlate; whether the therapeutic window permits repeated treatment at clinically relevant doses and schedules; and whether intervention yields reproducible intracranial responses, durable disease control, or survival benefit. Reproducible predictive and pharmacodynamic biomarkers support patient selection and assessment across these steps. Within this framework, we compare the distinct pharmacological and clinical implications of the blood-brain barrier/blood-tumor barrier, DNA damage response, cancer stem-like cell states, and immune evasion in GBM and brain metastases from lung cancer, breast cancer, and melanoma. We further examine the pharmacological rationale, maturity of evidence, and practical limitations of emerging approaches, including drug repurposing, antibody-drug conjugates, synthetic-lethal strategies, microenvironmental reprogramming, and rational combination therapies. Future progress will depend less on expanding the catalogue of resistance mechanisms than on embedding spatial pharmacokinetics, longitudinal molecular monitoring, and functional validation into clinical trials, thereby enabling mechanistic insights into resistance to be translated into specific, testable, and dynamically adaptable therapeutic decisions.

articles.title: Third-Line and Later Therapy for Metastatic Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis with Contextual Overview on Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Based Strategies in MSS/pMMR Disease.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Multiple third-line and beyond (3L+) treatments for metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) are available, yet no direct comparative evidence exists across all active regimens. TAS-102 ± bevacizumab, regorafenib, and fruquintinib have each demonstrated an overall survival benefit (OS). Recently, the first positive randomized data for an immune-checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-containing regimen in an unselected microsatellite-stable/proficient mismatch repair (MSS/pMMR) mCRC population were reported (STELLAR-303). OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy and safety of third-line and later-line therapies for MSS/pMMR mCRC using a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized trials, and to provide a contextual overview of ICI-based strategies. PATIENTS AND METHODS: We conducted a PROSPERO-registered systematic review and fixed-effects NMA of randomized trials in the 3L+ mCRC setting. Hazard ratios (HRs) for OS were extracted or derived from published reports and harmonized to a placebo/best-supportive care (PBO/BSC) reference using Bucher-anchored indirect comparisons. RESULTS: Thirteen trials formed a PBO/BSC-anchored, star-shaped OS network. Based on frequentist P-scores, TAS-102 plus bevacizumab ranked highest (0.99), followed by zanzalintinib plus atezolizumab (0.85), fruquintinib (0.68), and TAS-102 monotherapy (0.58). Regorafenib and other active regimens showed intermediate rankings, whereas atezolizumab monotherapy, nintedanib, and anlotinib ranked lowest. Pairwise relative treatment effects were generally consistent with the overall ranking pattern, although confidence intervals (CIs) overlapped for several treatment comparisons. CONCLUSION: TAS-102 plus bevacizumab was associated with the most favorable OS ranking, while zanzalintinib plus atezolizumab may represent a promising option. These findings support evidence-based sequencing of 3L+ therapies in mCRC and highlight the evolving role of multi-axis targeted and immune-modulatory strategies.

articles.title: Targeting zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 prevents osteoarthritic cartilage fibrosis and degeneration through epigenetically repressing the IL-17B/C/D pathway.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Accumulative evidence demonstrates that hyaline cartilage fibrosis and the resulting degradation of extracellular matrix are implicated in the pathology of osteoarthritis (OA). However, the mechanisms behind this remain largely undefined. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Zinc finger E-box binding homeobox 1 (ZEB1) was identified as the most up-regulated transcription factor during OA progression using a regulon specificity score analysis on the public single-cell RNA sequencing dataset of human knee-joint tissues. The functional role of ZEB1 in OA and the underlying mechanism were evaluated using both conditional knockout mice combined with multiple OA models and primarily cultured OA chondrocytes. Tissue-specific in vivo gene editing of ZEB1 was applied to investigate the therapeutic effect of pharmacological targeting of ZEB1 in OA mouse models. KEY RESULTS: ZEB1 is identified as an aberrantly activated transcription factor in the articular cartilage of human patients and mice with OA. Chondrocyte-specific and inducible deletion of ZEB1 in OA mice reduces hyaline cartilage fibrosis and degradation, osteophyte formation and joint inflammation, restraining OA progression. Mechanistically, loss of ZEB1 reduces histone acetylation on Il-17b/c/d and Il-17rb/rd promoters, thereby epigenetically repressing IL-17B/C/D signalling, a critical pathway that supports OA progression through up-regulating pro-fibrogenic and pro-inflammatory pathways. Treatment with recombinant IL-17D protein fully restores the impaired OA progression in ZEB1-deleted mice. The microneedle-lipid nanoparticle-mediated co-delivery of Cas9 mRNA and single-guide RNA achieves knee joint-specific in vivo gene editing of ZEB1, providing an effective protection against OA in mice. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: ZEB1 may serve as a promising therapeutic target for OA.

articles.title: Development of a human toxicokinetic model of glyphosate for interpreting biomonitoring data.
articles.abstract: Glyphosate is widely used, yet interpreting urinary biomonitoring data as a measure of absorbed dose from occupational and environmental exposure remains challenging because urinary levels are influenced by the route and time of exposure, as well as toxicokinetic processes. We developed a 21-compartment physiologically informed compartmental toxicokinetic model for humans that represents oral, dermal, and inhalation inputs, systemic distribution, limited conversion to aminomethylphosphonic acid, and urinary and fecal elimination. Parameterization combined physiological blood-flow constraints with optimization against serial urinary glyphosate profiles from 10 healthy adults who consumed 125-247 µg of glyphosate in a controlled meal. A local sensitivity analysis was used to prioritize fitted parameters, and multiple optimized parameter sets were retained to characterize the range of solutions compatible with each volunteer urinary profile. The model reproduced the time course of urinary amounts excreted per interval, excretion rates, and cumulative excretion. Across volunteers, the estimated fraction of glyphosate directed from the gastrointestinal lumen to feces was 0.951-0.979, whereas the fraction transferred to intestinal tissues was 0.007-0.046. The fraction transferred from hepatic blood to venous blood was 0.858-0.949, supporting rapid hepatic transit and limited hepatocellular uptake. The apparent renal-blood to renal-tissue fraction varied among volunteers (0.008-0.434) and was among the most influential parameters, reflecting the limited ability of urinary data alone to reliably estimate this parameter. In contrast, the renal-tissue to urine fraction (0.689-0.999) indicated that urinary excretion was the predominant modeled pathway of elimination from renal tissues. Multiple parameter sets fitted individual profiles, reflecting incomplete identifiability from urine-only data. This model provides a quantitative framework for linking serial urinary biomonitoring data to plausible absorbed doses. Its quantitative performance is currently best supported for oral exposure; additional controlled human data are needed to optimize the parameterization of the dermal and inhalation exposure pathways.

articles.title: In vivo evaluation of hepatotoxicity following 35-day repeated oral exposure to perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) in male Wistar rats.
articles.abstract: Perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) is a persistent contaminant that bioaccumulates through the food chain, posing severe human health risks including endocrine disruption and systemic metabolic disorders. However, the specific molecular thresholds and mechanisms underlying its 35-day repeated-dose hepatotoxicity remain poorly defined. To mimic human exposure and reflect conditions potentially associated with long-term PFNA bioaccumulation, male Wistar rats were exposed to PFNA via drinking water at doses of 0, 0.05, 0.5, and 2 mg/kg body weight/day for 35 days. Post-exposure analyses included blood biochemical and endocrine parameters, liver histopathology, hepatic lipid accumulation and quantification of oxidative stress markers, xenobiotic metabolism, activities of antioxidant defense enzymes, mitochondrial complexes I/II activity, and key gene expression related to antioxidant defenses, CYP450s and lipogenesis. PFNA induced progressive, dose-dependent liver damage, macrovesicular toxicant-associated fatty liver disease (TAFLD), and elevated oxidative stress. Xenobiotic detoxification was impaired, evidenced by reduced 7-ethoxycoumarin O-deethylase activity and CYP2C11 downregulation. Notably, the liver displayed a clear dose-dependent bioenergetic threshold: low and intermediate doses (0.05 and 0.5 mg/kg/day) activated adaptive defenses, increasing mitochondrial Complex II activity to sustain energy demands. Conversely, the 2 mg/kg/day dose triggered a severe bioenergetic collapse and metabolic exhaustion, overwhelming late compensatory responses including PPARα activation, lipogenic FAS suppression, and peak catalase activity. In conclusion, 35-day repeated oral PFNA exposure induces a dose-dependent shift from adaptive energetic defense to comprehensive hepatic metabolic collapse, providing critical insights into the toxicological risk assessment of bioaccumulative perfluoroalkyl substances.

An antiangiogenic embolic hydrogel for modulating post-embolization vascular remodeling in hepatocellular carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Transcatheter arterial embolization is the standard clinical therapy for highly vascularized hepatocellular carcinoma, especially in patients ineligible for surgical resection. However, its efficacy is often compromised by incomplete embolization or and ischemia-induced neovascularization post-embolization, leading to tumor recurrence and metastasis. Here, a silk fibroin-based hydrogel with antiangiogenic capacity, termed as Bev@SH, was proposed to promote complete vascular embolization. In this system, silk fibroin is incorporated with nanoclay particle to enhance the mechanical strength and plasticity. This not only enables its penetration into tumor microvessels for complete vascular embolization, but also inhibits the post-embolization tumor neoangiogenesis through the controlled release of loaded bevacizumab. As a result, Bev@SH demonstrated precise and efficient embolization of small arteries in vivo and induced selective ischemic necrosis within targeted regions. In the rabbit VX2 liver tumor model, Bev@SH treatment reduced tumor burden and suppressed VEGF-induced angiogenesis without apparent adverse effects, demonstrating its excellent therapeutic efficacy and favorable short-term biosafety. Consequently, we anticipate that our Bev@SH holds promise as a feasible antiangiogenic embolic alternative for hypervascularized tumor.

articles.title: Localized lipid nanoparticle delivery of membrane bound IL-12 and T cell engager mRNA potentiates adoptive cell therapy in solid tumors.
articles.abstract: Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), which includes T cell receptor (TCR), chimeric antigen receptor (CAR), and tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy, has emerged as a promising form of immunotherapy for the treatment of cancer, with multiple FDA approvals across the three classes. However, each class faces its own specific hurdles for the treatment of solid tumors. Here, we investigated whether intratumoral administration of mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encoding immune-stimulatory proteins would be a strategy to boost the efficacy of ACT for the treatment of solid tumors. As proof-of-concept to demonstrate the validity of this LNP strategy, we designed and validated mRNAs encoding a novel membrane-bound single-chain human IL-12 (mbIL-12) to reprogram the suppressive tumor microenvironment, as well as an anti-human mesothelin-CD3ε bispecific T cell engager (MSLN-TE) with the potential to address antigenic heterogeneity. We investigated intratumoral administration of mbIL-12 and MSLN-TE mRNA LNPs in the setting of the clinical stage NY-ESO-1 8F TCR, observing robust improvements in TCR T cell therapy efficacy upon intratumoral LNP administration in a murine xenograft model of human lung adenocarcinoma. While delivery of each mRNA construct individually improved TCR T cell therapy efficacy, combined delivery of both constructs resulted in an additive improvement in efficacy. This work sets the stage for the application of mRNA LNP technology to improve the efficacy of ACTs.

articles.title: SN-38 targets RPB4 to disrupt Pol II-mediated HIF-1α transcription and suppress glycogen synthesis in triple-negative breast cancer.
articles.abstract: Tumor hypoxia drives aggressive behavior in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet the downstream adaptive outputs that sustain tumor fitness and the pharmacologic entry points through which this program can be disrupted remain poorly understood. Here, through a functional screen in TNBC cells under hypoxia, we identify camptothecin (CPT)-class compounds as robust suppressors of hypoxia-responsive transcription. Transcriptomic and functional analyses converge on glycogen synthesis as a shared hypoxia-adaptive program, with hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α)-dependent glycogen synthase 1 (GYS1) expression promoting glycogen accumulation and hypoxic fitness. In TNBC xenografts, irinotecan suppresses the HIF-1α-GYS1-glycogen axis and reduces tumor growth. Mechanistically, by combining thermal proteome profiling, chemoproteomics, biophysical binding assays, cellular target-engagement analyses, and genetic rescue experiments, we identify RPB4, a core RNA polymerase II (Pol II) subunit, as a direct SN-38 target under hypoxia. SN-38 disrupts Pol II integrity and reduces its occupancy at the HIF1A promoter, thereby attenuating hypoxia-responsive transcription. These findings reveal a glycogen-linked hypoxia-adaptive program in TNBC and establish a RPB4-centered Pol II perturbation as an additional mechanism contributing to the effects of SN-38 under hypoxia.

articles.title: 5-HETE links alveolar epithelial ferroptosis to impaired neutrophil swarming in ARDS.
articles.abstract: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is characterized by profound immune heterogeneity, with dysregulated inflammatory responses shaping both tissue injury and host defense. While persistent inflammation contributes to lung parenchymal cell injury, whether and how the damaged alveolar niche reshapes local immune defense remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that defective neutrophil swarming constitutes a critical immune defect that hinders bacterial clearance in ARDS. Mechanistically, alveolar epithelial type II (AT2) ferroptosis is associated with increased 5-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (5-HETE), which suppresses NOTCH signaling in neutrophils, leading to reduced ITGB3 expression and defective swarming. Dietary omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (ω-3 PUFAs) reduce 5-HETE accumulation, thereby preserving neutrophil antibacterial function. Our findings identify an AT2 ferroptosis-5-HETE-NOTCH2 axis that links alveolar epithelial injury to defective neutrophil collective behavior and suggest a potential nutritional strategy to restore local host defense in ARDS.

articles.title: Co-expression of NKG2A-HLA-E and TIGIT-CD155 immune checkpoints is associated with immune dysfunction and poor survival in gastric cancer.
articles.abstract: The clinical significance of the NKG2A-HLA-E and TIGIT-CD155 immune checkpoint pathways in gastric cancer (GC) remains incompletely understood. We investigated their prognostic relevance and therapeutic potential using public datasets, a cohort of 195 patients, flow cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, multiplex immunofluorescence, and functional assays, with particular emphasis on cellular co-expression, spatial organization, and functional immune responses. HLA-E and CD155 expression was elevated in later-stage tumors, and concurrent high expression was associated with shorter overall and disease-free survival. Multivariable Cox regression identified the tumor-to-adjacent-normal HLA-E expression ratio as an independent prognostic factor. Flow cytometry linked NKG2A and TIGIT expression to distinct functional states of CD8⁺ T cells and NK cells from primary tumors and malignant ascites. Single-cell analyses revealed NKG2A and TIGIT co-expression in exhausted CD8⁺ T cell and CD56bright NK cell subsets, together with HLA-E and CD155 co-expression in tumor epithelial cells. CellPhoneDB analyses predicted potential ligand-receptor interactions between tumor cells and infiltrating lymphocytes. Multiplex immunofluorescence demonstrated HLA-E and CD155 co-expression in tumor cells and close spatial proximity between HLA-E⁺ tumor cells and NKG2A⁺ lymphocytes. In ex vivo assays, combining NKG2A blockade with TIGIT or PD-1 blockade enhanced lymphocyte anti-tumor responses and organoid killing, with additional benefits over selected monotherapies. HLA-E or CD155 knockdown also enhanced immune cell function without further benefit from corresponding receptor blockade. Together, these findings suggest complementary immunoregulatory pathways associated with immune dysfunction and poor survival in GC, warranting independent prognostic validation and further preclinical evaluation of combination checkpoint blockade.

articles.title: Wumei Wan and nonivamide alleviate mucosal barrier injury in experimental colitis through TRPV1-associated sensory neuron-epithelial signaling.
articles.abstract: Persistent colonic mucus barrier damage is a hallmark of ulcerative colitis (UC). Sensory neuron-epithelial signaling helps maintain this barrier, but its role in Wumei Wan (WMW)-mediated mucosal protection remains unclear. We investigated WMW using a repeated-cycle dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) mouse colitis model, primary dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, and LS174T cells. WMW reduced mucosal injury, goblet cell depletion, and mucus loss while restoring mucin 2 (MUC2) expression and barrier integrity. Colonic transcriptomics implicated transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1)-positive sensory neurons, while resiniferatoxin (RTX)-mediated functional ablation attenuated WMW-mediated protection. TRPV1 activation increased calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release from DRG neurons, while CGRP promoted Yes-associated protein (YAP) nuclear translocation and MUC2 expression in LS174T cells through receptor activity-modifying protein 1 (RAMP1)-associated signaling. CGRP receptor blockade and YAP-TEAD inhibition attenuated CGRP-induced MUC2 upregulation. Dual-luciferase reporter and chromatin immunoprecipitation assays supported TEA domain transcription factor 1 (TEAD1) binding to the MUC2 promoter. Nonivamide (pelargonic acid vanillylamide, PAVA), chemically annotated in WMW, interacted directly with TRPV1 and promoted CGRP release from DRG neurons. Conditioned medium from PAVA-treated DRG neurons enhanced MUC2 expression in LS174T cells, an effect attenuated by CGRP receptor blockade. PAVA alleviated DSS-induced mucosal barrier injury, with reduced protection after RTX pretreatment. Collectively, these findings support the involvement of TRPV1-associated sensory neuron-epithelial signaling in the protective effects of WMW on the colonic mucosal barrier, demonstrate a role for CGRP receptor-associated YAP-TEAD1 signaling in MUC2 transcriptional regulation, and identify PAVA as a candidate compound with TRPV1-interacting and mucosal protective activities.

articles.title: Serious Breaches in the European Union Under the Clinical Trials Regulation (EU) No 536/2014: A Systematic Analysis of Characteristics and Challenges.
articles.abstract: In the European Union, the reporting of serious breaches established by Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 represents major progress aimed at strengthening participant protection and ensuring data robustness throughout the EU. Namely, Article 52 of the Regulation introduces a mandatory reporting requirement for breaches likely to have a significant impact on participant safety or rights, or the trial data integrity. The reporting of serious breaches reinforces the sponsor's active responsibility for maintaining trial oversight and for timely communication with National Competent Authorities, aimed at ensuring adherence to regulatory requirements. This study provides the first systematic review of serious breaches notified under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, using Italy as a case study to analyze the notification patterns, typologies, timelines, and seriousness assessments. Although the dataset is limited to serious breaches received by Italy and may not be fully representative of all serious breaches reported across the EU, it provides insights into the characteristics and distribution of serious breaches under the Regulation. It also aims to support stakeholders in consolidating harmonized approaches. In total, 320 serious breaches across 235 trials from 116 sponsors were analyzed; leading categories were investigational medicinal product administration/dosing errors (n = 73) and informed consent issues (n = 59). Inter-sponsor variability and reporting delays were observed, along with inconsistencies in the assessment of breach seriousness, suggesting opportunities for further harmonization of serious breach management. Continued monitoring of the serious breaches reporting process by the National Competent Authorities and inspection feedback should support harmonized and proportionate Regulation implementation across the European Union.

articles.title: Model-Based Meta-Analysis of the Efficacy of Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide-Targeting Monoclonal Antibodies for Migraine.
articles.abstract: Migraine is a prevalent neurological disorder that significantly impairs quality of life and productivity. Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) targeting the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) pathway have been approved for migraine prophylaxis. However, comparative data on these agents are limited. Therefore, we conducted a model-based meta-analysis (MBMA) to indirectly compare the efficacy of erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and eptinezumab. A systematic literature review identified 28 randomized controlled trials involving these agents. A longitudinal model was developed to describe the changes in monthly migraine days (MMD) following treatment initiation, incorporating study-specific placebo effects and drug-specific treatment effects. The baseline MMD was included as a power covariate, and dosing regimen effects were included as drug-specific categorical covariates. Model performance was assessed using goodness-of-fit plots, visual predictive checks (VPC), and bootstrap validation (1000 replicates). All agents demonstrated a robust and enduring reduction in MMD. Excluding placebo effects, the estimated treatment effects under standard dosing regimens ranged from approximately -1.5 to -2.0 MMD across agents. Additional regimen-specific effects were identified for high-dose erenumab and eptinezumab, resulting in greater estimated reductions in MMD. This study suggests that anti-CGRP mAbs currently available in major markets (e.g., the United States, Europe, and Asia) provide clinically relevant reductions in MMD, with broadly similar efficacy observed across agents over the 6-month study period. These findings highlight the need for further research into the mechanistic and patient-specific factors influencing treatment response.

articles.title: Seen, Studied, Served: Closing the Evidence Gap in Understudied Populations.
Bevacizumab in first-line postoperative treatment of advanced ovarian cancer: from high-risk stratification to precision decision-making.
articles.abstract: Bevacizumab is an important component of first-line therapy for advanced epithelial ovarian cancer; however, the precise identification of patients who will benefit and how to optimize its use in the era of poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) remains a core challenge in clinical practice. This review systematically revisits the pivotal phase III trials GOG-0218 and ICON7, together with their inherent limitations, with a particular focus on the role of KELIM score as a dynamic marker of chemotherapy sensitivity in predicting bevacizumab efficacy. Based on the interaction test from GOG-0218, the available evidence suggests that BRCA/homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) status does not alter the single-agent activity of bevacizumab; however, these genetic markers remain crucial for guiding PARPi or combination regimens. A key clinical dilemma arises when patients with a BRCA mutation have already received bevacizumab during first-line chemotherapy: should bevacizumab be continued or discontinued during the maintenance phase? This review presents a preference analysis and individualized decision-making factors based on available indirect evidence and current guidelines. Finally, a clinical decision pathway that integrates KELIM assessment with HRD testing is proposed to provide an evidence-based reference framework for the rational use of bevacizumab in first-line advanced ovarian cancer.

articles.title: Nrf2-related pathogenesis of premature ovarian insufficiency and traditional Chinese medicine-based interventions.
articles.abstract: Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a complex reproductive disorder characterized by diminished ovarian reserve and impaired ovarian endocrine function before the age of 40 years. Increasing evidence indicates that oxidative stress plays a pivotal role in POI pathogenesis by inducing mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, inflammatory responses, ferroptosis, and granulosa cell apoptosis, ultimately accelerating follicular depletion. Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), a master regulator of cellular antioxidant defense, is essential for maintaining ovarian redox homeostasis and protecting reproductive function. Recent advances have demonstrated that traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), including herbal medicines, bioactive metabolites, classical formulations, and acupuncture therapies, exerts protective effects against POI by modulating Nrf2-associated signaling networks, thereby enhancing antioxidant enzyme expression, improving mitochondrial function, reducing oxidative DNA damage, suppressing inflammation and apoptosis, and preserving follicular development. This review summarizes the pathological role of oxidative stress and Nrf2 signaling in POI, and discusses the current progress of TCM interventions modulating the Nrf2 pathway, including their molecular mechanisms and therapeutic potential. Furthermore, the limitations of current research, including the lack of clinically representative models, limited understanding of molecular targets, and insufficient evidence from well-designed clinical studies, are highlighted. Future studies integrating multi-omics approaches, precision medicine, and evidence-based clinical trials are warranted to further elucidate the regulatory networks of TCM-mediated Nrf2 activation and promote the clinical translation of TCM strategies for POI prevention and treatment.

articles.title: High-dose administration of EGFR-TKIs for NSCLC patients: a literature review.
articles.abstract: High-dose EGFR-TKIs have been used as an exploratory therapeutic strategy to overcome the limitations of the standard-dose regimen in the treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC, particularly in patients with CNS metastases. Available clinical evidence suggests that high-dose TKIs confer certain therapeutic efficacy and manageable safety profiles, with a small proportion of patients experiencing ≥3 grade adverse events, such as rash, nausea,diarrhea, aminotransferase rise, leukopenia.However, the evidence is limited by the predominance of single-center retrospective studies, small sample sizes, heterogeneous patient populations and short follow-up periods. Further large-scale, multicenter studies with long-term follow-up are needed to define more clearly the efficacy, safety, and appropriate clinical role of high-dose EGFR-TKI therapy.

articles.title: Nanomedicine-enabled delivery of natural products targeting the Notch cascade: addressing translational barriers in cancer therapy.
articles.abstract: Notch signaling is a conserved cell-fate pathway that becomes therapeutically important when malignant cells use it to sustain stemness, epithelial plasticity, vascular remodeling, immune escape, and resistance to cytotoxic therapy. Natural products provide a chemically diverse source of Notch modulators, including polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and related phytochemicals that can influence receptor activation, nuclear Notch signaling, and downstream phenotypes. Their multi-target behavior is attractive in heterogeneous tumors, yet the same compounds often suffer from poor aqueous solubility, rapid metabolism, low systemic exposure, weak tumor accumulation, and formulation instability. Nanomedicine offers a practical route to re-engineer these compounds as therapeutic systems rather than isolated small molecules. Liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, solid lipid systems, hydrogels, biomimetic carriers, and stimulus-responsive platforms can increase bioavailability, prolong circulation, improve tumor localization, and support co-delivery with chemotherapy, nucleic acids, immunomodulators, or pathway inhibitors. This review summarizes the Notch cascade in cancer, representative natural products that modulate Notch-driven cancer phenotypes, pharmacokinetic barriers that restrict their translation, and nanomedicine strategies that may overcome these barriers. It also discusses active targeting of the Notch/cancer stem cell axis, biomimetic delivery, co-delivery systems for resistance reversal, and translational challenges involving nanotoxicity, manufacturing, advanced models, and systems-level evaluation.

articles.title: Are all adaptogens created equal? A comparative review and trend analysis of clinical data.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The use of adaptogenic ingredients in dietary supplements and herbal medicines is increasingly common. The pharmacological effects of generally acknowledged adaptogens at tissue and cellular levels through various mechanisms result in a range of clinically relevant effects, such as increasing resilience during the stress response, supporting more rapid recovery from stressors, and decreasing the intensity of post-stress exhaustion. While clinical effects for adaptogens should be non-specific, traditional use and commercial marketing suggest different applications for individual adaptogens. To this end, the authors conducted a comparative review of clinical research to test the hypothesis based on traditional understanding that adaptogen-specific effect profiles exist and that adaptogens have differentiable clinical relevance. METHODS: A comparative trend analysis of clinical evidence using accepted vote-counting methodology and data synthesis was conducted on seven generally acknowledged adaptogens: ashwagandha (Withania somnifera), schisandra (Schisandra spp.), eleuthero (Eleutherococcus senticosus), rhodiola (Rhodiola rosea), Asian ginseng (Panax ginseng), reishi (species of Ganoderma), and cordyceps (species of Cordyceps and Ophiocordyceps along with affiliated Paecilomyces hepiali). RESULTS: A total of 275 clinical studies were included and scored based on primary and secondary outcomes across seven clinical outcome domains: energy, cognition, mood, sleep, immunologic and inflammatory balance, cardiometabolic health, and the reproductive system. Trend analysis of this dataset identified which adaptogens showed significant positive directions of effect in each domain, and demonstrated some significant differences in clinical outcome distribution profiles for each adaptogen. DISCUSSION: Individual adaptogens show unique effect profiles measured by the outcomes of clinical research in diverse domains, corroborated by traditional use.

articles.title: Pharmacokinetics and bioequivalence of rasagiline mesylate tablets in healthy Chinese subjects under fasting and fed conditions: an open, randomized, single-dose, four-period crossover clinical trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: This clinical trial evaluated the pharmacokinetic profiles and bioequivalence of a generic rasagiline mesylate tablet versus the branded reference product in healthy Chinese subjects under fasting and fed conditions to support an abbreviated new drug application. Safety and tolerability were monitored throughout the study. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, randomized, open-label, four-period, two-sequence crossover trial in healthy Chinese participants. In each period, subjects received a single 1 mg oral dose of either formulation; plasma rasagiline concentrations were quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and pharmacokinetic parameters were derived by non‑compartmental analysis. Bioequivalence was assessed using either the reference-scaled average bioequivalence (RSABE) or the standard average bioequivalence (ABE), depending on the within‑subject standard deviation (SWR) of the reference formulation. RESULTS: A total of 64 subjects were enrolled and randomized (30 fasting, 34 fed). For peak plasma concentrations (Cmax), which exhibited high variability (SWR > 0.294), RSABE was used, while ABE was applied for AUC0-t and AUC0-∞. Under fasting conditions, the geometric mean ratio (GMR) of test/reference for Cmax was 109.80%; under fed conditions, it was 111.60%. The 95% upper confidence bounds for both conditions were less than zero. The 90% confidence intervals for AUC0-t and AUC0-∞ GMRs were 98.82%-107.11% and 98.96%-107.11% (fasting), and 96.92%-102.34% and 97.15%-102.64% (fed), all falling within the 80-125% acceptance range. No serious adverse events were reported. CONCLUSIONS: The test formulation met the bioequivalence criteria under both prandial states and was well tolerated, with a safety profile similar to that of the reference product. TRIAL REGISTRATION: The trial was first registered at chinadrugtrials.org.cn (CTR20230947, date: March 29, 2023) and subsequently retrospectively registered at chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR 2500099491, March 25, 2025).

articles.title: Formalizing combination therapy for resistant bacterial infections.
P2X7 Receptor at the Intersection of Alzheimer's Disease and Depression: Neuroimmune Mechanisms, Translational Evidence and Therapeutic Opportunities.
articles.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and depression often occur together in older adults, and their two-way clinical association is increasingly being documented as a probable factor contributing to cognitive and functional deterioration. Although these disorders differ in their clinical manifestations, converging evidence implicates neuroimmune dysregulation, microglial reactivity, oxidative and mitochondrial stress, and impaired synaptic plasticity in their pathophysiology. Purinergic P2X7 receptor (P2X7R), an ATP-gated cation channel that is particularly relevant to activated immune and glial cells, represents a potential molecular interface between these processes. This review critically examines evidence linking P2X7R signalling with AD and depression, emphasising on ATP-dependent ion flux, microglial activation, NLRP3 inflammasome signalling, inflammatory cytokines, oxidative and mitochondrial dysfunction, synaptic impairment, amyloid precursor protein processing, tau-associated pathology, and neuroplastic mechanisms. Rather than considering P2X7R involvement in two disorders independently, we distinguish direct evidence for AD-depression comorbidity from disease-specific evidence and from mechanistic extrapolations based on shared biological pathways. Preclinical studies indicate that P2X7R inhibition can attenuate neuroinflammatory responses and improve cognitive or depression-related behavioural phenotypes in experimental models. Early clinical studies of CNS-penetrant P2X7R antagonism demonstrate target engagement and modulation of inflammatory pathways, but clinical efficacy has not yet been established. Collectively, available evidence supports P2X7R as a biologically plausible neuroimmune convergence point between AD and depression, while highlighting important gaps in direct comorbidity models, human biomarkers, target engagement, disease-stage specificity and therapeutic efficacy. Addressing these gaps will be essential to determine whether P2X7R can progress from a mechanistically attractive target to a clinically actionable strategy for AD-associated depression.

articles.title: Decoding microglia-neuron crosstalk in epileptogenesis.
articles.abstract: Epileptogenesis is a complex, multifaceted process by which a normal brain undergoes structural and functional changes leading to the development of epilepsy. Historically, research has focused on neuronal mechanisms such as ion channel dysfunction and synaptic reorganization. However, a paradigm shift has occurred with the recognition that neuroinflammation and glial cells are fundamental contributors to this process. Central to this non-neuronal axis are microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, which engage in a dynamic, bidirectional dialogue with neurons. This review synthesizes current evidence indicating that microglia-neuron crosstalk serves as a critical driver of epileptogenesis and disease progression. It will explore how initial epileptogenic insults and neuronal hyperactivity, through signals like adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and fractalkine, instruct microglial activation. In turn, the review details how activated microglia profoundly influence neuronal excitability and circuit remodeling-both through the release of cytokines such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and through structural mechanisms including complement-mediated synaptic pruning and phagocytosis. It argues that this intricate communication loop creates a self-perpetuating cycle that fuels the epileptogenic cascade. Consequently, decoding this dialogue is not only crucial for understanding the underlying pathophysiology but also for developing novel, anti-epileptogenic therapies that move beyond symptomatic seizure suppression to directly target the disease progression.

articles.title: Lineage-state immunometabolism in thyroid cancer: a framework for pharmacological research.
articles.abstract: This critical narrative review synthesizes published genomic, metabolic, single-cell, spatial and clinical studies of thyroid cancer to examine how lineage, differentiation and treatment history condition immunometabolic observations. In follicular-cell-derived tumors, impaired iodine handling is associated with diverse changes in glucose use, mitochondrial function, amino-acid metabolism and redox control; specific perturbation studies establish causal relationships within defined models. Oncocytic thyroid carcinoma provides a mitochondrial counter-state, whereas medullary thyroid carcinoma belongs to a distinct parafollicular C-cell lineage. Human tissue associations, thyroid-model functional findings, cross-cancer mechanisms and clinical outcomes are distinguished at the level of individual claims. Selected immune circuits have functional support in thyroid models, while many proposed spatial metabolic exchanges remain inferential. Mitogen-activated protein kinase-directed redifferentiation can restore radioiodine uptake in selected refractory differentiated cancers, although uncontrolled treatment sequences do not isolate the added benefit of radioiodine. Established genotype-directed and biomarker-selected therapies are distinguished from investigational combinations, cellular therapy and hypothesized post-treatment metabolic changes. We propose a lineage-state framework to organize evidence, identify pharmacological questions and guide study design. Histology, genotype, imaging and clinical monitoring anchor its clinically established components; spatial, metabolic and model-supported assays require validation for their intended uses. The framework is an organizing heuristic, not a validated clinical treatment algorithm.

articles.title: Mitochondrial DNA in cancer: From molecular pathogenesis to clinical translation.
articles.abstract: As the only extra-nuclear genetic material, mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has transcended its traditional boundaries, emerging as a multifunctional regulator in cancer biology. This review provides a comprehensive synthesis of the expanding roles of mtDNA in malignancy, spanning from its intracellular functions to its clinical translational potential. MtDNA mutations and copy number alterations drive cancer progression by endowing cancer cells with enhanced proliferative capacity, metastatic fitness, and therapeutic resistance. These effects are primarily mediated through reprogramming oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), fine-tuning reactive oxygen species (ROS) homeostasis, and modulating mitochondrial integrity. As a signaling messenger, mtDNA leaked into the cytoplasm or extracellular space exerts dual functions: it can trigger anti-cancer immune responses by activating multiple signaling pathways, while also promoting cancer progression by mediating immune evasion and microenvironment remodeling within the cancer. The recent elucidation of horizontal mitochondrial transfer (HMT) expands the scope of mtDNA action from intracellular dynamics to intercellular communication, rendering functional mtDNA a transferable vehicle for metabolic reprogramming, immune modulation, and therapy resistance within the tumor microenvironment. In diagnostics, mtDNA abnormalities detected through liquid biopsy and mutation analysis offer promising biomarkers for early cancer detection. Therapeutically, small-molecule inhibitors, nanoparticle-based delivery systems, and G-quadruplex-targeting ligands disrupt mtDNA function through divergent mechanisms, presenting new avenues for clinical intervention. Collectively, these advances underscore mtDNA as a central node in cancer progression and a compelling target for next-generation diagnostics and therapeutics.

articles.title: Chrysanthemi flos and Ocular Health: An Ethnopharmacological Review from Traditional Use to Modern Evidence.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Chrysanthemi flos consists of the dried capitula of Chrysanthemum morifolium Ramat. (Asteraceae) and has long been used medicinally, as a tea, and as a dietary material. Its traditional oral and external applications, including the concept of "calming the liver and improving vision," provide an ethnopharmacological basis for evaluating its relationship with ocular health. AIM OF THE REVIEW: This review aims to integrate and critically evaluate the traditional uses, phytochemical basis, contemporary experimental evidence, and safety data related to Chrysanthemi flos and ocular health from an ethnopharmacological perspective. By incorporating ocular compartment characteristics and the HMR-350 cross-species functional reference framework, it establishes an evidence framework for evaluating the potential relevance of Chrysanthemi flos to ocular health. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A structured, critical narrative review approach was adopted. PubMed, Web of Science, and CNKI were searched for studies published between 1990 and 2026, supplemented by classical Chinese medical texts, the Chinese Pharmacopoeia, and reference-list screening. The search focused on "Chrysanthemum morifolium," "Chrysanthemi flos," the names of the nine representative bioactive compounds, and terms related to ocular health and safety. Original studies with defined test materials, experimental models, intervention conditions, and major outcomes were prioritized, and evidence was integrated according to test-material source and ocular compartment. Eye development-related genes were retrieved using Gene Ontology/AmiGO 2, and orthologous mapping across humans, mice, and rats was performed using Ensembl BioMart to construct the HMR-350 gene set as a cross-species functional reference. RESULTS: Historical materia medica texts and modern pharmacopoeias have documented ocular-related uses of Chrysanthemi flos, providing an ethnopharmacological basis for its modern evaluation of ocular health. Phytochemical studies indicate that flavonoids and phenolic acids are among the most extensively investigated constituent classes in C. morifolium. Based on the available phytochemical evidence and ocular-related research, this review focuses on nine representative bioactive compounds. Modern evidence spans three ocular compartments-the ocular surface, intraocular contents, and fundus-and is predominantly derived from cell-based and animal studies. Studies directly evaluating chrysanthemum-derived materials remain relatively limited, whereas evidence from purified compounds accounts for a substantial proportion of the literature. Cross-species analysis identified HMR-350, comprising eye development-related genes shared by humans, mice, and rats, and further organized these genes into five mechanistic reference modules: redox homeostasis and antioxidant defense; inflammation and immune regulation; neuroprotection and visual function; tissue homeostasis and barrier-ECM-vascular processes; and apoptosis/autophagy and cell survival. Available safety data encompass animal toxicology, human exposure, local tolerability, potential interactions, exogenous contamination, and gastrointestinal digestion and metabolism, providing preliminary evidence for the safety assessment of chrysanthemum-derived materials. CONCLUSION: This review establishes an integrated analytical framework encompassing traditional uses, bioactive constituents, ocular compartment-specific evidence, the HMR-350 cross-species functional reference framework, and safety evaluation. This framework provides a basis for understanding the potential links between Chrysanthemi flos and ocular health and for further evaluating its potential for development as an ocular health-related functional food. Future studies should prioritize standardized characterization of raw materials, assessment of constituent exposure, and human intervention studies to facilitate the translation of the available evidence into practical applications.

articles.title: ​Integrating implementation science in psychedelic-assisted therapy research: translational research methods and design considerations.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Psychedelic-assisted therapy has demonstrated efficacy in several conditions-particularly major depression and posttraumatic stress disorder-but limited implementation research may risk compromising the translation of these interventions into real-world clinical practice. OBJECTIVES: Here, we identify frameworks and methods from implementation science that could be incorporated into upcoming phase 2-4 clinical trials of psychedelic-assisted therapy to inform the translation of ​ these interventions into real-world practice. RESULTS: Hybrid Type 1 trials could fill the present implementation research gap in PAT by simultaneously evaluating clinical efficacy or effectiveness, while collecting implementation data. Informed by implementation frameworks and principles, we propose two distinct prototype Hybrid Type 1 trials-a traditional two-arm effectiveness trial and a factorial optimization trial-to facilitate data collection and analyses that could inform future clinical and early implementation research. CONCLUSIONS: The present co​mmunication offers a starting point for clinical researchers to identify accessible concepts, ​frameworks, and methods that could be incorporated in upcoming effectiveness and implementation research of psych​edelic-assisted therapy. The proposed research designs integrate effectiveness- and implementation approaches to support the systematic evaluation of psychedelic interventions across diverse clinical settings. Implementation considerations could inform clinical development and refinement of psychedelic-assisted therapy, while the timing and intensity of formal implementation research should reflect the maturity of the intervention and the decisions that can meaningfully be addressed at each stage.

articles.title: Clinical translation of viral targeting of the endothelium in pulmonary vascular diseases.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary vascular diseases are characterized by endothelial dysfunction and progressive vascular remodeling. Most pulmonary vascular diseases, such as pulmonary hypertension, are rare but fatal. Although current therapies improve hemodynamics and clinical outcomes, they do not consistently restore endothelial homeostasis or reverse vascular remodeling, highlighting the potential of gene therapy as a disease-modifying strategy. AREAS COVERED: This narrative review examines the pulmonary vascular endothelium as a therapeutic target and discusses its heterogeneity, disease-dependent targetability, and its interactions with the other components of the vascular wall. We review adeno-associated viral, adenoviral, lentiviral and bocaviral vectors, including capsid/envelope engineering, receptor-mediated targeting, transcriptional and post-transcriptional restriction, and delivery routes. Therapeutic strategies such as gene replacement, transcription-factor delivery, and gene suppression are discussed, with particular emphasis on BMPR2. Translational barriers including viral vector immunity, species-dependent tropism, biodistribution, durability, controllability, manufacturing, and patient selection are also considered. EXPERT OPINION: Pulmonary endothelial gene therapy represents a highly promising but clinically immature approach. Progress will depend on vectors that achieve selective transduction of pulmonary endothelial cells while minimizing off-target accumulation. Improved preclinical models including large animals or human tissue may guide vector development. Novel targeted vectors will enable effective gene transfer, thereby reducing dose and vector-based immunotoxicity.

articles.title: Effects of efflux transporter genes on irinotecan-induced hematologic toxicity: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: AIM: Irinotecan is an anticancer drug used to treat colorectal and other solid tumours. Despite its efficacy, it has severe toxicities, including neutropenia and diarrhoea. The genetic association of UGT1A1 with irinotecan toxicity is reflected in Food and Drug Administration (FDA) drug labels; however, the effects of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter gene polymorphisms remain unclear. Therefore, this meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the genetic effects of ABC transporters on irinotecan-related hematologic toxicity. METHODS: Relevant studies were searched on PubMed, SCOPUS and Web of Science. The meta-analyses were conducted using the Mantel-Haenszel method and the z-test. Heterogeneity was assessed using Higgins' I2 statistic. A random-effects model was employed to provide a more conservative effect. RESULTS: A total of 19 studies were included. Rs2032582 in ABCB1 was associated with a reduced risk of irinotecan-induced hematologic toxicity (OR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.25-0.91). Rs2292997 in ABCC5 and rs225440 in ABCG1 were related to increased risks of toxicity (OR = 2.05, 95% CI: 1.23-3.43 and OR = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.00-3.25, respectively). CONCLUSION: In conclusion, ABC transporter gene polymorphisms, particularly rs2032582 in ABCB1, may contribute to interindividual variability in hematologic toxicity of irinotecan. These findings may contribute to personalized therapy of irinotecan, after prospective validation.

articles.title: Implementation pathway of NAT2 genotype-guided isoniazid dosing in tuberculosis.
articles.abstract: N-Acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2) is a major determinant of isoniazid exposure and contributes to clinically important variability in drug response during tuberculosis treatment. The poor-metabolizer phenotype is associated with increased isoniazid exposure and a higher risk of anti-tuberculosis drug-induced liver injury, whereas the rapid-metabolizer phenotype is associated with reduced exposure and potentially unfavourable treatment outcomes. However, NAT2 genotype-guided dosing has not been widely implemented in routine care. In this narrative review, we summarize the biological, pharmacokinetic and clinical evidence for NAT2 and compare the translational pathways of TPMT-thiopurines, SLCO1B1-statins, CYP2C19-clopidogrel, DPYD-fluoropyrimidines and NAT2-hydralazine to identify considerations relevant to implementing NAT2-guided isoniazid dosing. These examples demonstrate that pharmacogenomic prescribing guidance and clinical implementation do not follow a single linear pathway and that initial prescribing recommendations have sometimes been developed without definitive randomized trial evidence. Importantly, the evidence needed to support prescribing guidance differs from that required to establish the clinical utility of routine testing. For NAT2, priorities include defining actionable phenotype-specific dosing and monitoring strategies; evaluating the complete test-to-treatment pathway; and generating further evidence on clinical effectiveness, feasibility and economic value across diverse settings. Carefully governed regional implementation with prospective evaluation, together with targeted comparative studies, may help strengthen the evidence base for future pharmacogenetic prescribing recommendations and the incorporation of NAT2 testing into clinical practice guidelines.

articles.title: Breaking barriers: advanced targeted drug delivery strategies for sensorineural hearing loss.
articles.abstract: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is the most prevalent form of hearing impairment worldwide. However, drug delivery to the inner ear is severely hindered by the enclosed bony labyrinth and the highly selective blood-labyrinth barrier (BLB), resulting in suboptimal therapeutic outcomes and confining pharmacological management largely to symptomatic rather than etiological intervention. This review systematically dissects the multifaceted barriers to inner ear drug delivery and focuses on three core strategic pillars: (i) optimization of administration routes to balance invasiveness with cochlear bioavailability; (ii) rational selection of viral and non‑viral vectors guided by the unique pharmacokinetic properties of inner ear fluids; and (iii) functional modification of delivery systems with cell‑specific ligands to achieve precision targeting.Particular emphasis is placed on breakthrough advances such as LRP1‑mediated noninvasive trans-barrier delivery and prestin‑targeting peptide‑directed selective outer hair cell engagement. By integrating insights from drug delivery science, gene therapy, and targeted delivery research, this review proposes a conceptual framework to facilitate the clinical translation of precision medicine for SNHL. This narrative review synthesizes evidence from 189 peer-reviewed articles identified through a systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase databases (published between 1984 and 2026, focusing on advanced strategies to overcome the blood-labyrinth barrier (BLB).

articles.title: Differential metabolic impacts of a modified traditional Japanese diet and the DPP-4 inhibitor alogliptin on uric acid dynamics in drug-naïve subjects with type 2 diabetes.
articles.abstract: Uric acid (UA) is traditionally regarded as a metabolic risk marker; however, its dynamic behavior during glucose-lowering therapy remains incompletely understood. We investigated the effects of a modified Japanese diet for diabetes (MJDD) and the DPP-4 inhibitor alogliptin on UA dynamics in subjects with early-stage T2DM. In this non-randomized, prospective observational study, drug-naïve patients received MJDD (n = 58) or alogliptin (n = 52) monotherapy for 3 months. Changes (Δ) in serum UA were analyzed in relation to glycemic control, insulin resistance, adipo-IR, and beta-cell function. Both interventions significantly reduced FBG and HbA1c while paradoxically increasing serum UA and HOMA-B. Baseline UA was the primary determinant of ΔUA in both cohorts. MJDD significantly reduced BMI, insulin, FFA, HOMA-R, and adipo-IR, with effects most pronounced in subjects with baseline BMI ≥ 25. In contrast, alogliptin selectively reduced adipo-IR in leaner subjects (BMI < 25). Across both treatments, ΔUA correlated positively with ΔHOMA-B and inversely with ΔHbA1c. Notably, during MJDD, ΔUA showed a paradoxical negative correlation with ΔBMI and ΔFBG, and a positive correlation with ΔFFA. Subjects exhibiting the greatest UA increases demonstrated the most marked improvements in HOMA-B and, with MJDD, the greatest weight loss. These findings indicate that MJDD and alogliptin exert distinct metabolic effects in early T2DM, yet both link rising UA to enhanced HOMA-B, suggesting that UA may serve as a dynamic pharmacometabolic biomarker reflecting therapy-specific metabolic changes.

articles.title: Ferroptosis-related molecular signatures in Alzheimer's disease and the neuroprotective effects of allicin: an integrated bioinformatics, peripheral single-cell transcriptomic, and experimental study.
articles.abstract: Ferroptosis is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the relationship between AD-associated transcriptomic changes, peripheral immune alterations, and candidate ferroptosis-modulating compounds remains incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify ferroptosis-related molecular signatures associated with AD and to evaluate whether allicin attenuates ferroptosis-related injury in complementary experimental models. Human hippocampal microarray datasets GSE1297 and GSE28146 were examined with explicit consideration of donor overlap; GSE1297 was treated as the primary subject-level reference dataset, whereas the donor-overlapping GSE28146 dataset was used only as a cross-platform sensitivity source and not as an independent cohort. Ferroptosis-related candidates were prioritized using FerrDb, AD-related annotation, protein-protein interaction analysis, and pathway analysis. Peripheral-blood single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE181279) were analyzed to describe immune-cell composition and peripheral distribution of candidate genes without extrapolating these findings to brain-parenchymal cell localization. Candidate-drug prediction and molecular docking were followed by D-galactose/AlCl3 rat experiments and erastin-treated PC12-cell experiments. Histology, ROS, Western blotting, RT-qPCR, and JC-1 assays were used to assess ferroptosis-related molecular and mitochondrial changes. Ferroptosis-focused transcriptomic screening and network prioritization highlighted GPX4, FSP1, SLC7A11, TFRC, and ACSL4 as candidate genes for subsequent analyses. Their expression pattern was compatible with reduced antioxidant defense and increased iron/lipid-peroxidation susceptibility in AD-associated hippocampal transcriptomes. Peripheral single-cell analysis showed heterogeneous expression of these genes across T-cell, B-cell, NK-cell, monocyte, and platelet populations; these results are interpreted as peripheral immune context rather than evidence of brain-cell localization. Molecular docking predicted energetically favorable allicin-protein poses, but does not establish direct target engagement. In the experimental models, allicin attenuated histopathological injury and ROS accumulation, shifted GPX4, FSP1, SLC7A11, TFRC, and ACSL4 expression in an anti-ferroptotic direction, and improved mitochondrial membrane-potential readouts, with changes directionally similar to ferrostatin-1. The combined data support an association between AD-related molecular changes and ferroptosis-regulatory pathways and show that allicin can reduce ferroptosis-related injury in the models used. Because the human datasets include donor overlap, the single-cell dataset is peripheral rather than brain-derived, and direct target-engagement, lipidomic, genetic-rescue, and pharmacokinetic experiments were not performed, the findings should be considered mechanistically suggestive rather than proof that allicin directly targets the five proteins or specifically inhibits AD-associated ferroptosis in humans.

articles.title: Icariin targets Rho family GEF FARP2 to modulate GTPase signaling for neuroprotection.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Oxidative stress is a primary driver of neuronal injury in neurodegenerative conditions including ischemia stroke (IS). Icariin (ICA), a natural flavonoid, exhibits neuroprotective activity. However, its direct molecular target remains elusive. Here, we identified the direct protein target of ICA and elucidated the downstream pathways mediating its protection against hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)-induced neuronal injury. METHODS: Neuronal B35 cells were treated with H2O2 to induce oxidative stress. Cell viability was evaluated using CCK-8 assays and Calcein-AM/PI double staining. The direct binding target of ICA was screened by drug affinity responsive target stability-mass spectrometry (DARTS-MS) proteomics, followed by validation through molecular docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations as well as cellular thermal shift assay coupled with Western blot (CETSA-WB). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) was performed to identify involved the signaling pathways. Network pharmacology and machine learning approaches including LASSO, random forest, and support vector machine, were applied to identify hub genes associated with IS. Finally, WB, phalloidin staining and siRNA-mediated FARP2 knockdown rescue experiments were performed to confirm the effects and mechanism of icariin in IS. RESULTS: ICA dose-dependently restored B35 cell viability following H2O2 exposure. FARP2 was identified as a direct binding target of ICA. Molecular docking and MD stimulations validated stable ICA-FARP2 binding (ΔG_bind = -21.38 ± 2.19 kcal/mol) driven by van der Waals and electrostatic interactions with Thr914 and Gln907. Transcriptomic profiling indicated that H2O2 exposure upregulated RhoGTPase signaling, extracellular matrix organization, and cilium assembly pathways. Integrated analyses further identified caspase-3 as a core regulatory gene and implicated Rap1 and PI3K-Akt signaling in IS. Finally, the functional validation confirms that FARP2 siRNA blocks the protective effect of icariin against H2O2-induced B35 cell injury. Conclusion: ICA exerts neuroprotective effects against H2O2-induced neuronal injury by targeting FARP2 and modulating RhoGTPase and PI3K-Akt signaling, suggesting its potential in regulating cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular stress responses.

articles.title: Insulin-sensitizing effects of Monascuspilosus ΔMpclr4 fermentation products: a strain- and time-dependent metabolomic and phenotypic stuy with candidate mechanisms.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Monascus fermentation products have hypoglycemic and lipid-lowering effects, but the influence of strain and fermentation time on metabolite profiles and insulin resistance (IR) improvement remains unclear. Uninoculated substrate showed no activity, confirming that bioactivity depends on microbial transformation, though the key metabolites and pathways are not fully known. METHODS: Untargeted LC-MS-based metabolomics was employed to profile the metabolite composition of fermentation products from two Monascus strains, ΔMpclr4 and MS-1, at 7, 14, and 21 days. Key metabolic pathways were identified through multivariate statistical analysis and KEGG pathway enrichment. An insulin resistance model was established in HepG2 cells using 250 μM palmitic acid to evaluate the activity of the fermentation products, and their effects on cell function and protein expression were assessed by CCK-8 assay, 2-NBDG glucose uptake, intracellular TC/TG measurement, and Western blotting. RESULTS: Metabolomic data exhibited good quality with clear group separation. Comparisons (MS-1-21d vs. control, ΔMpclr4-21d vs. control, and MS-1-21d vs. ΔMpclr4-21d) identified 1,516, 1,439, and 333 differential metabolites (VIP>1, FDR<0.05, |log2FC|>0.263), mainly enriched in tryptophan metabolism and steroid hormone biosynthesis. Among the three time points, ΔMpclr4-21d showed the most pronounced glucose uptake improvement and lipid reduction, surpassing the 14-day product. At 21 days, ΔMpclr4-21d showed more favorable effects than MS-1-21d on cell viability, glucose uptake, and intracellular TC/TG. In the cell assays, ΔMpclr4-21d significantly enhanced glucose uptake and lowered both TC and TG, whereas MS-1-21d only reduced TG and did not improve TC. ΔMpclr4-21d was associated with upregulation of 5-HT1A and PRLR and downregulation of GANAB. CONCLUSION: Monascus fermentation products were associated with amelioration of insulin resistance and with enrichment of pathways such as tryptophan metabolism and steroid hormone biosynthesis. However, the metabolomic data were obtained from the fermentation products themselves, not from treated HepG2 cells. The differential expression of 5-HT1A, PRLR, and GANAB is therefore proposed as correlates rather than direct evidence of intracellular pathway modulation. The ΔMpclr4 product fermented for 21 days exhibited the greatest activity among the three time points. These findings provide preliminary evidence for developing Monascus-based functional foods; however, direct mechanistic evidence and pathway intervention experiments are required to establish causality.

articles.title: HDAC6 inhibition reverts docetaxel resistance in castration resistant prostate cancer.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) represents a lethal stage of the disease for which docetaxel (Dtx), a microtubule-stabilizing agent, remains a standard-of-care therapy. However, the rapid emergence of docetaxel resistance severely limits its clinical benefit. Given that histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) is a central regulator of microtubule dynamics via α-tubulin deacetylation, we hypothesized that selective HDAC6 inhibition could re-sensitize CRPC cells to Dtx. METHODS: To elucidate mechanisms driving resistance and identify actionable vulnerabilities, we established docetaxel-resistant models in two different CRPC cell lines (DU145 and 22Rv1). We evaluated the inhibitory activity and cellular target engagement of 9b, a previously developed hydroxamic acid-based 1-benzhydryl piperazine derivative, using enzymatic assays and cellular thermal shift assays (CETSA). Functional assays and RNA sequencing were performed to investigate the effects of HDAC6 inhibition on docetaxel sensitivity and associated molecular mechanisms. RESULTS: Enzymatic assays demonstrated that 9b potently inhibits HDAC6 (IC50 = 0.031 μM) while exhibiting lower activity against class I HDACs, including HDAC1, HDAC3, and HDAC8. Consistently, CETSA revealed preferential target engagement of HDAC6 in the cellular environment, supporting its selective HDAC6-binding profile. Functionally, 9b significantly induced α-tubulin acetylation, enforced G2/M cell cycle arrest, and impaired CRPC cell migration. Notably, combined treatment with 9b and Dtx elicited caspase-dependent synergistic cytotoxicity, effectively reversing Dtx tolerance in resistant CRPC models. Consistent with this model, genetic ablation of HDAC6 similarly sensitized resistant cells to Dtx in colony formation assays. Mechanistically, RNA sequencing revealed that HDAC6 inhibition by 9b markedly suppressed MYC-driven transcriptional programs. DISCUSSION: These results implicate MYC signaling as a downstream effector of HDAC6-mediated Dtx resistance. Together, these findings demonstrate that 9b is a potent and selective HDAC6 inhibitor that enhances docetaxel response in resistant CRPC models. Furthermore, our results identify HDAC6 as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in docetaxel-resistant CRPC and provide a rationale for further evaluation of selective HDAC6 inhibition in more clinically relevant models.

articles.title: A novel icariside II derivative YS-10 exerts therapeutic effects on radiation-induced testicular damage via Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 mediated apoptosis restraint.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Previous studies have reported that YS-10 has shown potential in ameliorating radiation-induced injury and diabetic erectile dysfunction. Nevertheless, its protective effects against radiation-induced testicular injury and the underlying mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated. METHODS: In this study, we aimed to explore the protective effect of YS-10 against radiation-induced testicular injury. Male Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats were subjected to a single dose of 20 Gy X-ray irradiation (2 Gy/min dose rate) to establish the in-vivo testicular radiation-injury model; GC-2 cells were exposed to a single dose of 8 Gy X-ray irradiation (2 Gy/min dose rate) to construct the in-vitro testicular radiation-injured cell model. RESULTS: YS-10 treatment elevated sperm concentration and viability in irradiated rats and ameliorated testicular inflammatory response. Functional enrichment analysis revealed that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) from testicular specimens were markedly and uniquely enriched in signaling pathways related to oxidative stress and apoptosis. Compared with the Model group, YS-10 treatment significantly suppressed Keap1 expression, facilitated Nrf2 activation and upregulated HO-1 expression. In vivo and in-vitro functional assays verified that YS-10 markedly reduced the proportion of TUNEL-positive cells, decreased intracellular ROS levels, promoted cell proliferation, rescued the collapse of mitochondrial membrane potential, upregulated anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 expression and suppressed pro-apoptotic Bax expression. Furthermore, treatment with an Nrf2 inhibitor in vitro attenuated the protective effects of YS-10. CONCLUSION: Collectively, YS-10 significantly ameliorates radiation-induced damage in testicular tissues and GC-2 cells. Suppression of apoptosis and activation of the Keap1/Nrf2/HO-1 signaling axis are associated with the protective effects exerted by YS-10.

articles.title: An interpretable XGBoost model for predicting measured teicoplanin plasma concentrations in ICU patients with bloodstream infection: a two-center real-world validation study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Profound pharmacokinetic variability complicates individualized teicoplanin therapy in critically ill patients with bloodstream infection. We aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable machine learning (ML) model for predicting teicoplanin plasma concentrations in this population.
